items.title: Copernicus, the Tusi Couple and East-West Exchange in the Fifteenth Century
items.venue: Unifying Heaven and Earth (Universitat de Barcelona), 19–58
items.note: Surveys fifteenth-century contacts between Byzantine, Islamic and Latin scholars as plausible channels by which the Ṭūsī couple could have reached Copernicus.

items.title: Ibn al-Shāṭir and Copernicus: The Uppsala Notes Revisited
items.venue: Journal for the History of Astronomy
items.note: Re-reads Copernicus's notes in an Uppsala volume and argues that Ibn al-Shāṭir's models had features that made them useful for a heliocentric transformation.

items.title: Copernicus's Derivation of the Heliocentric Theory from Regiomontanus's Eccentric Models of the Second Inequality of the Superior and Inferior Planets
items.venue: Journal for the History of Astronomy
items.note: Traces the heliocentric step to Regiomontanus's eccentric models in the Epitome, a Latin source route that does not depend on Maragha material.

items.title: Nicolaus Copernicus' books digitized
items.note: The Copernicana collection, books from Copernicus's library with his annotations, put online in full, opening the marginalia used in transmission arguments to direct inspection.

items.title: From Tūn to Toruń: The Twists and Turns of the Ṭūsī-Couple
items.note: Traces versions of the Ṭūsī couple across Arabic, Greek, Hebrew and Latin sources and the routes by which they could have reached Europe.

items.title: La Nihāya al-sūl fī taṣḥīḥ al-uṣūl d'Ibn al-Shāṭir: édition, traduction et commentaire mathématique
items.note: Critical edition and French translation of Ibn al-Shāṭir's main theoretical treatise, with reconstruction of its models, giving an openly available base text for comparison with Copernicus.

items.title: Where Did Copernicus Obtain the Tools to Build His Heliocentric Model? Historical Considerations and a Guiding Translation of Valentin Rose's "Ptolemaeus und die Schule von Toledo" (1874)
items.note: Translates Rose's 1874 study of Toledan transmission and revisits Iberian and Latin channels through which Arabic geometrical devices might have reached Copernicus.

items.title: Abner of Burgos: The Missing Link between Nasir al-Din al-Tusi and Nicolaus Copernicus?
items.note: Proposes a Hebrew route via a fourteenth-century Castilian text describing a Ṭūsī-type device.

items.title: A Rebuttal of Recent Arguments for Maragha Influence on Copernicus
items.note: Replies to Ragep, Barker and Heidarzadeh, and Bala, maintaining that no documentary route has been shown and that independent invention remains adequate.

items.title: The Mercury Models of Ibn al-Šāṭir and Copernicus
items.who: S. Nikfahm-Khubravan and F. J. Ragep
items.note: Argues from detailed model structure and parameters that Copernicus's Mercury model is too close to Ibn al-Shāṭir's to be independent.

items.title: L'ombre de la science arabe : dans les marges de la bibliothèque de Copernic
items.note: Reviews the Maragha-transmission dispute through the books and marginalia surviving from Copernicus's library.

items.title: Out of Maragha: Observations, Teachings, and Translations
items.note: Places the late thirteenth-century Greek translations of Maragha and Tabriz astronomy in the teaching practice of those centres, the start of the Byzantine route.

items.title: Islamic Astronomy and Copernicus
items.note: Open-access collection of fifteen of Ragep's articles making the case for an Islamic background to Copernicus's models.

items.title: The Origin of the Reciprocation Device in Copernicus: Proclus In and Ṭūsī Out
items.note: Argues from Copernicus's allusion to Proclus's Euclid commentary and from Rheticus that the reciprocation device came via the Proclus tradition and Paduan astronomers, not Maragha.

items.title: Merchants of Knowledge: Intellectual Exchange in the Ottoman Empire and Renaissance Europe
items.note: Book-length study of Jewish and other intermediaries, including Moses Galeano, who carried Islamic astronomy between the Ottoman world and Italy around 1500.

items.title: An Unknown Astronomical Work on Planetary Theory from the Renaissance: Giulio Cesare Luchini's Delle revolutioni delle sfere celesti libri IX (ca. 1581)
items.who: P. D. Omodeo and R. S. Mousavi
items.venue: Journal for the History of Astronomy
items.note: Studies a Paduan manuscript adapting Copernicus's reciprocation mechanism, evidence for how the device was understood and circulated in the Veneto.
